items.originalTitle: ‘They should be subsidizing the ratepayers’: NC governor says data center subsidies should be rolled back
items.author: Jessica Piper
items.title: ‘They should be subsidizing the ratepayers’: NC governor says data center subsidies should be rolled back
items.summary: North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein said his state needs to roll back subsidies for data centers, telling POLITICO that Big Tech companies should be “paying their own way.” “I think the idea that this industry needs any public incentive is laughable. These are the wealthiest companies in the history of humanity. They have more resources than many nations. So we, little North Carolina, should not be giving subsidies,” Stein said in an interview Thursday at the POLITICO Pub at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. The Democratic governor pointed to subsidies in North Carolina for electricity for data centers that were rolled back earlier this year , along with ongoing subsidies for the purchase of new equipment, which he said ought to be phased out. “For new data centers, why are we giving them any public dollar when they should be subsidizing the ratepayers?” he said. Stein, elected in 2024, will be governing with a divided Legislature next year after Democrats flipped North Carolina’s House of Representatives this year and broke the Republican supermajority in the state Senate amid a nationwide blue wave . Republicans are likely to maintain narrow control of the upper chamber pending a recount in a pivotal race. The first-term governor, who won by nearly 15 points in 2024 despite President Donald Trump also winning the state that year, didn’t commit to running again in 2028 but said he “cannot think of any” reasons not to. Stein touted bipartisan work in the state to address recovery from Hurricane Helene, which devastated western North Carolina in 2024. But he faulted “one of the most ineffectual Congresses in history” for failing to deliver for the state. The $60 billion in damages North Carolina suffered, he noted, are nearly as large of a sum as the state’s two-year budget — making it impossible for the state to allocate enough funds for recovery. He said that he spoke to Trump earlier this year and was told that hurricane recovery was a priority for the president, but the necessary federal funds have not come through. “The state stepped up,” Stein said. “The people of Western North Carolina have truly stepped up, and it's time for the federal government to step up.”

items.originalTitle: Nevada's new governor promises legislative blitz on affordability
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.title: Nevada's new governor promises legislative blitz on affordability
items.summary: Nevada Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford is vowing to immediately pass a trifecta of measures that he says will drive down the cost of living when he enters office in the key swing state. “Those are concrete things that immediately can bring some level of effect to this cost-of-living crisis that we're experiencing right now,” Ford told POLITICO’s Megan Messerly in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. The legislative blitz includes a bill to make school breakfast and lunch free for public school students, legislation that would limit the cost of prescription drugs to the Medicare-negotiated price for everybody and new rules aimed at lowering housing costs that would limit the number of homes corporations can purchase. “I've been working with my colleagues already in the Legislature, and we're going to sign bills beginning on Day 1,” Ford said. “We'll be signing bills within the first 30 days to ensure that we can start effectuating some of the promises that I made on the campaign trail. “You hear people signing executive orders to make things easier for businesses — cut regulations and make it easier to do business — I think that’s cool, that’s fine, and that’s dandy. But if you could do it for businesses, you could do it for people too,” he also said. The incoming Nevada governor and former state attorney general also emphasized his willingness to work across the aisle — even though the massive Democratic wins in his state earlier this month make it so “I don't need one Republican vote to get something done in my state right now,” he said. Nevada will be the second state to vote in the Democratic primaries in 2028, and Ford said candidates need to come and travel up and down the state before staking out policy positions. “You need to come to Nevada. Period. Point blank,” Ford said. “We’re one of the most diverse states in the nation. If you can convince a Nevadan that you’re worth your salt, you may very well be able to convince the rest of the nation that you are.” And he cautioned Democrats against making assumptions on what Nevadans want and need. “Don’t presume you know what their issues are,” he said. “Don’t be high and mighty and highfalutin and sitting in some ivory tower putting out ideas when you haven’t heard them say to you what their concerns are.”

items.originalTitle: JD Vance slams GOP governor’s call for immigration reform as ‘morally and electorally disastrous’
items.author: Lauren Fedor and Neha Sati
items.title: JD Vance slams GOP governor’s call for immigration reform as ‘morally and electorally disastrous’
items.summary: Vice President JD Vance took aim at Kevin Stitt, calling the Republican governor of Oklahoma’s push for bipartisan immigration reform “morally and electorally disastrous.” “I like Kevin, but what does ‘bipartisan immigration reform’ mean?” Vance wrote on X on Thursday morning. “If you mean making it harder for megacompanies to defraud our visa system, great. If you mean we should pass legislation to make it harder for employers to violate our immigration law, I'm all ears,” Vance wrote. “But to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws. It is morally and electorally disastrous.” The vice president was responding to comments the Oklahoma Republican made at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Park City, Utah, on Wednesday. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt said. Stitt described President Donald Trump as a “businessperson” who “understands the need for a workforce.” “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy,” the Oklahoma governor said. But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It’s not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they’re winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That’s why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.” Asked about Vance’s comments on Thursday, Stitt told POLITICO he was “super pumped that the vice president is being engaged in the conversations.” “The governors have been leading on this,” Stitt added. “Republican governors, Democrat governors, have a lot to say on immigration policy, and I am glad the vice president is listening.” Stitt has long called for sweeping changes to immigration policy, including enabling state governors to issue work permits to unauthorized immigrants. Vance – who is weighing a run for the White House in 2028 – has been a staunch defender of the Trump administration’s aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration. Trump has signaled he is open to cutting a deal on immigration reform in the wake of his party’s midterm defeats. The president told CBS News’s “60 Minutes” earlier this month that his deportation policy was “ too tough ” and had hurt Republicans with some midterm voters. But any agreement still seems unlikely. The same day he spoke to “60 Minutes,” Trump named immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff. Asked about the possibility of a deal earlier this week, Trump told reporters at the White House: “It would be wonderful, but we’ll see.” The president said any agreement would “have to be tough” and offer “no amnesty” for unauthorized immigrants.

items.originalTitle: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
items.author: Adam Wren
items.title: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
items.summary: Allies of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are launching an independent, grassroots effort urging him to undertake a second presidential campaign ahead of 2028. Team Pete PAC will be led by Jennifer Holdsworth, the former national campaign manager of Buttigieg’s unsuccessful 2017 bid for DNC chair, and Mohsin Syed, his former chief of staff at the Transportation Department. The PAC is aiming to bring together volunteers and grassroots donors who backed Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential bid. “Mohsin and I have traveled the country this year, and everywhere we go, people ask us the same question: how can I help Pete?” Holdsworth said in a statement. Team Pete PAC is independent and has no ties to Buttigieg’s Win the Era PAC, nor is it a presidential committee. Through Win the Era, Buttigieg campaigned with 102 candidates across the map for the midterms, visiting 38 states (19 of them twice). Asked on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday whether he had a timeline to make a decision, Buttigieg said he would be “surprised” if he was the first potential 2028 presidential candidate “to make news” and said he’s “certainly not cooking up anything to announce in the next few weeks.” Even as it forms to press Buttigieg to mount a second presidential campaign, Team Pete PAC is urging potential backers to take part in community service — a nod to Buttigeig’s proposed national service program he proposed as a candidate. “I’ve seen up close what Pete can do,” Syed said. “He has a unique ability to bring people together and inspire action.”

items.originalTitle: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
items.author: Willie D. Jones
items.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
items.summary: Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job. Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension , CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there. Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan County Title Extension regional specialist Member grade Senior member Alma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products. Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business. She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside. “We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in. Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and the U.N.’s International Telecommunication Union , and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC) , and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP). She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture . An early love of design and problem-solving Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors. As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs. That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings. “I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says. She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career. She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University , in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education. She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016. That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry , in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020. From outreach to extension work After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College , in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator. She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water. She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain , helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park. In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County ’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns. She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds. Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System , a nationwide network run by land-grant universities , schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states. The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture , managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties. The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program , which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship. Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person. She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says. “We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says. Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI . The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly. How her AI chatbot helps farmers and ranchers In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree , in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global . She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python , a popular programming language . It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT ’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it. The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download. Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk. One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch , in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases . Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication. Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) . The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing. She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude , and Gemini . She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp ., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp ., Colorado Startup Week , and Boulder Startup Week . And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel. Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools , she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use. She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says. Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.” How IEEE membership supports her career Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology . She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group . IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences. IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.” She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE. Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone. “They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

items.originalTitle: Sonos is taking up to 30 percent off speakers and soundbars right now
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.title: Sonos is taking up to 30 percent off speakers and soundbars right now
items.summary: The excellent Sonos Play offers up to 24 hours of playback on a single charge. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge Sonos speakers and soundbars aren’t exactly cheap, but thankfully the company’s Black Friday sale has already begun , making everything a little easier to afford through November 30th. Most notably, you can pick up the Arc Ultra soundbar for a new low of $849 ($250 off) from Sonos , Amazon , and Best Buy , or the newfangled Sonos Play for $239 ($60 off) from the same retailers ( Sonos , Amazon , Best Buy ). If you’re looking to give your home theater setup a big upgrade, the Arc Ultra is an excellent soundbar. It supports Dolby Atmos and delivers more immersive sound than the original Arc , while adding Bluetooth connectivity. Dialogue also sounds noticeably clearer, and the new Quick Tune feature automatically adjusts the soundbar’s audio to suit your room using built-in microphones, so you no longer need an iPhone to fine-tune the sound for your environment. For more powerful bass, you can also pair it with a compatible Sonos subwoofer, like the Sub 4, which is also available from Sonos as part of a discounted bundle for $1,499 ($499 off) . Read our full Arc Ultra review . Sonos Arc Ultra Where to Buy: $1099 $849 at Amazon $1099 $849 at Sonos $1099 $849 at Best Buy If you’re looking for a more affordable soundbar, the second-gen Sonos Beam has also hit a new low price at Amazon , Best Buy , and Sonos’ online storefront , where you can buy it for $339 ($160 off). The sound isn’t quite as immersive as that of the Arc Ultra, but the latest Beam can still fill a room with rich, clear audio. It also supports Dolby Atmos; however, unlike the newer Beam Ultra , it lacks side- and upward-firing speakers and instead relies on software to replicate surround sound effects. It also supports HDMI eARC, providing high-quality audio from a compatible TV. Read our Sonos Beam (second-gen) review . Sonos Beam (Gen 2) Where to Buy: $499 $339 at Amazon $499 $339 at Sonos $499 $339 at Best Buy If you’re shopping for a smart speaker instead of a soundbar, the Era 100 SL is available for an all-time low of $149 ($40 off) from Sonos , Amazon , and Best Buy (the standard Era 100 is also down to $179 at Amazon and Best Buy ). The feature-packed speakers are nearly identical, but the SL model lacks a built-in mic, and thus voice controls. Both offer excellent stereo sound and rich bass, with dual tweeters and a large woofer that delivers clear, detailed audio despite its small size. They also support Bluetooth and Apple’s AirPlay 2, and you can connect a wired audio source like a turntable using an optional USB-C adapter . For a more immersive experience, you can even pair two for stereo sound or use them as rear surrounds with a compatible Sonos soundbar. Read our Sonos Era 100 review . Sonos Era 100 SL Where to Buy: $189 $149 at Amazon $189 $149 at Sonos $189 $149 at Best Buy Sonos Era 100 Where to Buy: $219 $179 at Amazon $219 $179 at Sonos $219 $179 at Best Buy If you want a speaker you can take on the go, the newer Sonos Play is available from Sonos , Amazon , and Best Buy for $239 ($60 off), which is the first notable discount we’ve seen. The portable speaker delivers clear, detailed sound that can fill both larger rooms and outdoor spaces. It also offers up to 24 hours of battery life and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance, making it a great companion for long days at the beach or other outdoor adventures. Plus, its removable carrying loop makes it easy to bring along, and you can even use it to top off your phone. Like other Sonos speakers, it supports both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and you can also group it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when you’re outdoors and away from Wi-Fi. Read our Sonos Play review . Sonos Play Where to Buy: $299 $239 at Amazon $299 $239 at Sonos $299 $239 at Best Buy Last but not least, you can also buy the Sonos Ace for $229 ($120 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , and directly from Sonos , which marks a new low price. The newer Ace Ultra offer better sound and improved noise cancellation, but the Ace is still a solid option, especially if you already own a Sonos soundbar. The gorgeous headphones deliver powerful, detailed sound, solid noise cancellation, and an exceptionally natural-sounding transparency mode, along with up to 30 hours of continuous playback on a single charge. Unlike the newer Ultra, though, they can’t transfer music from your other Sonos speakers to your headphones. However, their TV Audio Swap feature still lets you transfer audio from a compatible Sonos soundbar to your headphones, so you can watch movies or listen to music playing on your TV without disturbing anyone else. Read our Sonos Ace review . Sonos Ace Where to Buy: $399 $229 at Amazon $399 $229 at Sonos $399 $229 at Best Buy

items.originalTitle: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite hasn’t been this cheap since June
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.title: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite hasn’t been this cheap since June
items.summary: alt: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is just $10 more than the base model alt: The last-gen Kindle Paperwhite for $130 is a stellar Black Friday deal Amazon debuted its latest Kindle Paperwhite in October, which is now available for $199.99 and replaces the outgoing 2024 model. However, given the minimal improvements on the new model — it’s a little thinner and opens books faster — the last-gen Paperwhite is still one of the best e-readers you can buy. And now, the latter is down to $129.99 ($70 off), nearly its lowest price ever, at Amazon , Best Buy , and Target . Some important pricing context: The waterproof e-reader held steady at $159.99 until late August, when its price rose 25 percent due to rising component costs ( many other Amazon tech products got more expensive, too). Even if the price hike never happened, though, this would still be a nice discount. Kindle Paperwhite (2024) Where to Buy: $199.99 $129.99 at Amazon (with ads) $199.99 $129.99 at Best Buy (with ads) $199.99 $129.99 at Amazon (with ads) The $129.99 Paperwhite includes 16GB of storage and features lockscreen ads (it costs $20 extra to opt out at checkout), just like the newer version. It also packs a sharp 300ppi display with adjustable color temperature and USB-C charging. If you want more features — including twice the storage, zero ads, wireless charging, and an auto-adjusting front light — opt instead for the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition while it’s down to $179.99 (also $70 off), which is just $10 shy of its best price to date. For the sake of being comprehensive, the last-gen base Kindle is going for $119.99 ($30 off) at Amazon ahead of Black Friday. While the standard Kindle has improved with each new iteration, it’s tough to recommend when the vastly superior Paperwhite is on sale for just $10 more. That 10 bucks gets you so much: waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).
